lesson.title: Setting up the practice set
lesson.skill: Set up one equation for a problem you actually have to solve, before trying to solve it.
lesson.missionLink: This is the first fifteen minutes of the Friday deadline. Everything after it is faster if you do this part first.

primarySource.why: Same method as the concept lesson, at practice pace.

content.text: A hands-on lesson is a checklist, not an explanation. Work down it with your actual problem set open, and tick each step as you go.

blocks.title: Set up problem one, end to end

items.instruction: Copy problem one onto a clean page and write the sentence it is actually about.
items.check: You have one written sentence in front of you that does not contain an equals sign.

items.instruction: Name the unknown with one letter, and write what it measures underneath.
items.check: A single letter and a plain phrase sit next to each other, and the letter appears in no other role.

items.instruction: Write the equation both ways round, once for each way you could read it.
items.check: Two equations, and at least one of them has the unknown on both sides.

items.instruction: Say the equation out loud as a sentence about the quantities.
items.check: You can say it without reading it, and what you say sounds like arithmetic rather than like a formula.

content.text: If your equation needs the unknown on both sides, stop. Go back to the word problem: there is usually a second unknown you have not named.
An equation you can say out loud in plain words is an equation you can solve. If you cannot, it is not finished.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, why does the sentence come before the equation?
blocks.modelAnswer: Writing the sentence first fixes what the unknown measures. The equation is then a translation of that sentence, so a wrong equation shows up as a sentence that no longer matches the problem.
rubric: Says the sentence pins down what the unknown is
Says the equation translates the sentence
